transcript:
This message comes from Schwab. At Schwab, you can get everything from self-directed investing to full-service wealth management, all in one place.
No matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how, you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Dale Willman. Leaders of the world's most advanced economies, the G7, say they'll coordinate to release 100 million barrels of crude oil over the next four months.
The deal includes a substantial release of diesel fuel within the first 20 days. It's an effort to stabilize prices and ensure supply.
As NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports, French President Emmanuel Macron called the G7 meeting after pressure from the Trump administration.
President Trump had threatened to stop exports of U.S. diesel entirely in an attempt to lower U.S. prices ahead of the midterm elections.
French President Emmanuel Macron has previously said such a move would be a catastrophe.
European governments are also under huge pressure from their populations as the price of gas and diesel skyrockets.
The G7 leaders said they agreed on the coordinated measures that would help stabilize energy supplies, shield households and businesses from price shocks, and strengthen the long-term resilience of global energy systems.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Paris.
The Labor Department said Friday that employers slowed their job hiring last month, adding just 29,000 jobs.
That was fewer than economists had expected and a slowdown from August's rate of 133,000. Gus Fauchet is the chief economist for the PNC Financial Group.
He says the news is actually a good thing for the economy.
The reason it rose is because we had more people looking for work over the month. That's actually a good sign.
We've seen fewer people looking for work in recent months, in part because of restrictions on immigration.
But if we see more people entering the labor force, more people looking for work, that means they're encouraged by the job market.
New York Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul says she wants answers about why an alleged rape case at Cornell University wasn't fully investigated.
NPR's Brian Mann has more.
Hochul says she's troubled by the behavior of university leaders, campus police, and a local prosecutor who dropped the investigation two years ago after seeing only a partial transcript of the woman's allegations.
I will not allow anyone to sweep this case under the rug.
Letitia James, the state attorney general, will now take over the criminal probe.
Hochul says she'll also push to close a loophole in state law that makes it harder to prosecute sex crimes when the victim has been drinking or using drugs.
Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape, period.
Cornell University has also agreed to Hochul's demand that an outside counsel review the school's handling of the case.
Brian Mann, NPR News, Ithaca, New York.
Russian attacks on Ukraine have forced the partial closing of three of the six bridges over the Dnipro River in the capital of Kiev.
The closings have caused major traffic jams in the city.
It appears to be an escalation in Russia's attacks, which has usually focused on apartment blocks, gas stations, data centers, and energy infrastructure.
This is NPR News.
Krista Pike was unconscious for hours after her failed execution in Tennessee Wednesday.
That's according to her attorneys, who said in a court filing Friday that hospital staff were trying to save her life by clearing her system of the drug used for the execution attempt.
The attorneys say they believe problems with the IV lines caused the drug to flow into her body rather than her bloodstream.
Much of Southern California is under an extreme heat warning at this hour.
Downtown Los Angeles hit 102 degrees on Friday, breaking a previous record for the day in 1955.
As L.A.U., member station LAist reports, forecasters say the heat wave could last for a week or longer.
Temperatures are expected to be in the mid-90s to mid-100s in greater Los Angeles, even in coastal areas.
Ryan Cattell is a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.
He says it's likely the heat wave will extend into the second week of October.
Unfortunately, you don't really see an end to it as far as we can tell.
And that's probably the biggest thing we want to highlight, is that while we have had hotter events this season already, this one might be the longest lasting.
Cattell says with the heat comes the high risk of fire.
Southern California Edison says thousands of customers are under consideration for power shutoffs to reduce the risk of electrical equipment sparking of fire.
For NPR News, I'm L.E.U. in Los Angeles.
Former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Tony Romo has been forced out at CBS Sports.
He has been the lead game analyst for CBS's NFL coverage since 2017.
He had been under suspension for the past month after pleading no contest to charges of operating a vehicle while intoxicated.
He was arrested in July in Wisconsin.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.
